Because it is difficult, great compassion grows and the practice of the vow becomes firm; because it is easy, the mind of compassion is not deep and the practice of the vow is not broad. The Larger Amitābha Sutra says "one day of cultivation in this world surpasses one kalpa of cultivation in the Western Pure Land" — it is precisely on account of this. Moreover, this Sahā world is the place where one was born in the past; the connections must surely be many, and the transforming of them is urgent. Therefore, having been born in the Pure Land, one must first return here. Question: Why not simply transform and guide sentient beings right here in this world — what is wrong with that? Why must one leave this and go there, and only then return? Answer: If one does not leave this world, then one is liable to fall; where could transforming and guiding begin? If one does not go there, then self-benefit is not yet accomplished; how could one secure benefiting others? It is like a poor man who has not yet seen the emperor nor received office — he himself is too busy with hunger, cold, and want to provide for his neighbors and townsfolk. Hence one knows: if one is unwilling to deliver sentient beings, that is that; if one is willing, then one must seek the West. If one is not born in the West, that is that; having been born there, one must return. Question: Just now one wished to be reborn there, and now wishes to return — is this not a hesitant advance and retreat, an undecided will? Answer: The earlier stage seeks self-benefit, therefore one vows to be reborn there; the later stage wishes to benefit others, therefore one must return. Though the resolve is made at one time, the action has a sequence. If one did not first make this intention, then once born in the Pure Land, returning would be difficult — what then of the four kinds of kindness and the three realms? Hence one knows: before attaining rebirth, one is resolved never to beget the thought of again entering the womb; having been born in the Land of Peace and Nurture, one is resolved never to lack the mind of coming back to transform and guide. This precisely shows the certainty. How can one call it undecided? (Therefore, before one has been reborn, one has already resolved never again to give rise to the thought of entering the womb; and being born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one is resolved never to lack the mind of returning to the Sahā world to transform and guide sentient beings. This is precisely the certainty of the intention; how can one call it undecided?)

Question: In the West one does not regress; but if one returns to the Sahā world, is there still regression? Answer: As made clear above, the three bodies and four wisdoms and the rest appear in full, and moreover with Amitābha's protective mindfulness and the Buddhas' sustaining, how can there be any principle of regression! It is like returning to one's home village wearing brocade, plying the oars with a following wind — no seeking that is not advantageous, no going that does not advance. The Bodhisattva's delivering of sentient beings is necessarily preceded by seeking rebirth in the West before returning — indeed for this reason."

Master Xing'an's Commentary on the Western Pure Land Text says: "Such great vows — this sums up the preceding text. 'Worlds inexhaustible' and the rest are examples used to state, in summary, that my vow is inexhaustible. As when it is said: the worlds cannot be exhausted, therefore my vow cannot be exhausted; sentient beings cannot be exhausted, karma and afflictions cannot be exhausted, therefore my vow cannot be exhausted; if these four could be exhausted, then my vow could be exhausted. Question: Why set forth this inexhaustible vow? Answer: Because mind is inexhaustible; the vows one makes in accordance with the mind are likewise without end. Moreover, 'worlds...' and the other four all exist within the mind; even upon becoming a Buddha, there is no principle by which they could be exhausted. Question: Since the vow is inexhaustible, when will one become a Buddha? Answer: What is called 'becoming a Buddha' is only recognizing that one's own mind in the end does not arise. As for the thirty-two marks, which are skillfully displayed as a matter of convenience — they are in themselves not real; what is there to discuss of accomplishment and non-accomplishment?"
